claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV with a neuron-specific promoter specifically labels CSF-cNs in Pkd2l1-Cre mice.
source: We first found that intracerebroventricular injection of adeno-associated virus with a neuron-specific promoter and Pkd2l1-Cre mice specifically labeled CSF-cNs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and validation of this labeling method with immunohistochemical confirmation of PKD2L1 co-expression.

claim: Single-cell labeling revealed that CSF-cNs have rostral axon extensions of over 1800 μm in unmyelinated bundles in the ventral funiculus.
source: Single-cell labeling of 71 CSF-cNs revealed rostral axon extensions of over 1800 μm in unmyelinated bundles in the ventral funiculus and terminated on CSF-cNs to form a recurrent circuitry, which was further determined by serial electron microscopy and electrophysiology.
evidence: The manuscript presents single-cell tracing data with measurements of axon lengths from 71 traced cells.

claim: CSF-cNs form recurrent connections with other rostrally located CSF-cNs.
source: Single-cell labeling of 71 CSF-cNs revealed rostral axon extensions of over 1800 μm in unmyelinated bundles in the ventral funiculus and terminated on CSF-cNs to form a recurrent circuitry, which was further determined by serial electron microscopy and electrophysiology.
evidence: The manuscript provides anatomical tracing, electron microscopy, and electrophysiological evidence of recurrent connections.

claim: CSF-cNs connect with axial motor neurons around the central canal and within the axon bundles.
source: CSF-cNs were also found to connect with axial motor neurons and premotor interneurons around the central canal and within the axon bundles.
evidence: The manuscript presents anatomical data showing connections between CSF-cNs and retrograde-labeled motor neurons.

claim: CSF-cNs connect with premotor interneurons around the central canal and within the axon bundles.
source: CSF-cNs were also found to connect with axial motor neurons and premotor interneurons around the central canal and within the axon bundles.
evidence: The manuscript shows anatomical connections with Chat+ and Chx10+ interneurons.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of CSF-cNs reduced speed and step frequency during treadmill locomotion.
source: Chemogenetic CSF-cNs inactivation reduced speed and step frequency during treadmill locomotion.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data from DREADD-mediated inactivation experiments with kinematic analyses.

claim: CSF-cNs are located in the subependymal area of the central canal in the spinal cord and caudal medulla in vertebrates.
source: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) are functionally enigmatic cells located in the subependymal area of the central canal in the spinal cord and caudal medulla in vertebrates (Orts-Del'Immagine and Wyart, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CSF-cNs have bulbous dendritic structures containing motile cilium and microvilli that extend apically into the CSF.
source: They have bulbous dendritic structures containing motile cilium and microvilli that extend apically into the CSF.
evidence: This is a description of known CSF-cN morphology from established literature.

claim: CSF-cNs are conserved in over 200 vertebrate species.
source: The broad conservation of CSF-cNs in over 200 vertebrate species implicates their fundamental physiological functions (Agduhr, 1922; Agduhr, 1932; Kolmer, 1921).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: PKD2L1 is expressed in CSF-cNs of mice, zebrafish, rabbits, and macaque monkeys.
source: The polycystic kidney disease 2-like 1 channel (PKD2L1), a member of the polycystin subgroup of transient receptor potential channels, was originally found to be expressed in the CSF-cNs of mice, and thereafter in other species including zebrafish, rabbits, and macaque monkeys (Djenoune et al., 2014; Tonelli Gombalová et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PKD2L1 is a chemo- or mechanosensitive nonselective cation channel that can sense extracellular pH, osmolarity, and mechanical flows.
source: PKD2L1 is a chemo- or mechanosensitive nonselective cation channel that can sense extracellular pH, osmolarity, and mechanical flows (Delmas, 2004; Orts-Del'immagine et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CSF-cNs physiologically respond to alkalinization and acidification in rodents and lampreys.
source: Indeed, CSF-cNs physiologically respond to alkalinization and acidification in rodents and lampreys, in which acid-sensing ion channel ASICs also contribute to lowered pH (Huang et al., 2006; Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Marichal et al., 2009; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2016; Orts-Del'immagine et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: CSF-cNs respond to osmolarity and ATP in rodents and fluid movements in lampreys.
source: CSF-cNs also respond to osmolarity and ATP in rodents and fluid movements in lampreys (Jalalvand et al., 2016b; Marichal et al., 2009; Orts-Del'immagine et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CSF-cNs are GABAergic interneurons that express glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) and GABA.
source: CSF-cNs have also been reported to be GABAergic interneurons that express glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) and GABA (Barber et al., 1982; Djenoune et al., 2014; Stoeckel et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs are mechanosensory neurons that detect intraspinal mechanical signals to control body posture and locomotion.
source: They showed that CSF-cNs are mechanosensory neurons that detect intraspinal mechanical signals to control body posture and locomotion in zebrafish (Böhm et al., 2016; Hubbard et al., 2016; Wyart et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to zebrafish studies.

claim: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs detect spinal bending through PKD2L1 and control tail beating locomotion.
source: In particular, CSF-cNs detect spinal bending through PKD2L1 and control tail beating locomotion (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a zebrafish study.

claim: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs send GABAergic inhibitory signals onto glutamatergic V0-v, CoPA interneurons, and CaP axial motor neurons.
source: They send GABAergic inhibitory signals onto glutamatergic V0-v (premotor descending), commissural primary ascending (CoPA) interneurons, and caudal primary (CaP) axial motor neurons (MNs) in local motor circuits to modulate locomotion and control balance during slow and fast swimming (Fidelin et al., 2015; Hubbard et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to zebrafish studies.

claim: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs contribute to the maintenance of spine curvature by sensing contacts with the Reissner fiber in the central canal.
source: CSF-cNs further contribute to the maintenance of spine curvature by sensing contacts with the Reissner fiber in the central canal (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020; Sternberg et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to zebrafish studies.

claim: In lampreys, CSF-cNs respond to spinal bending and pH alteration, leading to a decrease in locomotor burst.
source: These properties are partially observed in lampreys, in which CSF-cNs respond to spinal bending and pH alteration, leading to a decrease in locomotor burst in an isolated spinal cord (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to lamprey studies.

claim: AAV-labeled cells mostly co-expressed PKD2L1 throughout the rostrocaudal axis of the spinal cord (cervical 99.2±0.49%, thoracic 93.4±0.67%, lumbar 97.3±0.61%).
source: We found that the AAV-labeled cells mostly co-expressed PK2DL1, a specific marker of CSF-cNs, throughout the rostrocaudal axis of the spinal cord (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D; PK2DL1+/mCherry+: cervical, 99.2 ± 0.49%; thoracic, 93.4 ± 0.67%; lumbar, 97.3 ± 0.61%; n=4) (Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative immunohistochemical data showing co-localization percentages.

claim: AAV mostly labeled the ventral CSF-cN population rather than the dorsolateral ones (cervical 80.0±5.50%, thoracic 95.3±0.38%, lumbar 88.5±2.41%).
source: AAV mostly labeled the ventral cell population, rather than the dorsolateral ones (cervical, 80.0 ± 5.50%; thoracic, 95.3 ± 0.38%; lumbar, 88.5 ± 2.41%; n=4; Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the distribution of labeled cells.

claim: A neuron-specific promoter is required for specific CSF-cN labeling.
source: This indicates that a neuron-specific promoter is required for specific CSF-cN labeling.
evidence: The manuscript shows that AAV with CAG promoter labeled non-specific cells including ependymal and meningeal cells.

claim: CSF-cNs project fibers into the restricted area of the ventral funiculus and form large bundles.
source: We first observed that, in transverse sections, the cells projected fibers into the restricted area of the ventral funiculus and formed large bundles (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopic images showing fiber projections.

claim: The axons in the ventral bundles exhibited bouton-like structures and were labeled with presynaptic markers GAD65, GAD67, and VGAT.
source: The axons in the bundles exhibited a bouton-like structures in transverse sections. We stained the sections with presynaptic markers of inhibitory neurons: GAD65 (GAD2), GAD67 (GAD1), and VGAT. They showed a unique staining accumulated in the ventral mCherry+ fiber clusters (Figure 1E), which was consistent with the GABAergic properties of CSF-cNs (Djenoune et al., 2014; Stoeckel et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data showing co-localization with inhibitory markers.

claim: CSF-cNs are mutually aligned on each side of the spinal cord and extend dendritic bulbs that occupy most of the ventral surface of the central canal.
source: In the subependymal area, the cells are mutually aligned on each side of the spinal cord, and extended dendritic bulbs that were precisely aligned and occupied most of the ventral surface of the central canal (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopic images of horizontal sections showing cell alignment.

claim: Unique rostrocaudally projecting fiber bundles are located just beneath the ependymal cells, primarily observed at the cervical cord.
source: We further identified unique rostrocaudally projecting mCherry+ fiber bundles located just beneath the ependymal cells (Figure 1F, arrowheads). These subependymal bundles were also labeled by GAD65 and were primarily observed at the cervical cord, but not at other spinal levels (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopic images showing subependymal bundles.

claim: Most CSF-cNs had a single elongated axon that first projects ventrally and then rostrally in the ventral funiculus.
source: Most of the cells had a single elongated axon that first projects ventrally and then rostrally in the ventral funiculus (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents single-cell tracing data from 71 cells.

claim: All traced CSF-cNs projected to a specific side of the ventral funiculus without bilateral projections (left side 46.5%, right side 53.5%).
source: All of them projected to specific side of the ventral funiculus without bilateral projections (left side, 46.5%; right side, 53.5%), although it was unclear if they extended to ipsi- or contralateral side because their soma were located at the ventral midline along the central canal (67/71 cells).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from single-cell tracing.

claim: A small proportion of CSF-cNs exhibited caudal projections (4.2% in total) or bidirectional projections at the cervical level (1.2%).
source: A small proportion of the cells at the cervical and sacral levels also exhibited caudal projections in the ventral funiculus (4.2% in total) or bidirectional projections at the cervical level (1.2%; two cells at C2 and C4/5, respectively, with three and one cells located ventral and lateral to the central canal; Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from single-cell tracing.

claim: CSF-cN fibers extended rostrally to an average length of approximately 1800–4800 μm and tended to be longer in lumbar spinal cord.
source: Most of the fibers extended rostrally to an average length of approximately 1800–4800 μm and tended to be longer in CSF-cNs located in the lumbar spinal cord (Figure 2I).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative measurements of axon lengths from traced cells.

claim: Rostrally extending fibers had several dorsal collaterals that turned back to the central canal.
source: We further found that rostrally extending fibers had several dorsal collaterals that turned back to the central canal (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E; Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents single-cell tracing data showing collateral projections.

claim: CSF-cN fibers terminated in the region surrounding the central canal with abundant branching, extending to ipsi- and contralateral sides (ipsilateral 7.0%, bidirectional 62.8%, contralateral 9.3%, midline 20.9%).
source: The fibers terminated in the region surrounding the central canal with abundant branching fibers, extending to the ipsi- and contralateral sides in substantial population (ipsilateral, 7.0%; bidirectional, 62.8%; contralateral, 9.3%; midline beneath the central canal, 20.9%).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on terminal projection patterns.

claim: Dorsal collaterals were more abundant in cells of the cervical cord than in those of the caudal spinal cord.
source: These collaterals were more abundant in cells of the cervical cord than in those of the caudal spinal cord (Figure 2I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I-L).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data comparing collateral numbers across spinal levels.

claim: The cell bodies of GFP+ CSF-cNs frequently received contacts from tdTomato+ fibers that ascended dorsally.
source: We found that the cell bodies of GFP+ CSF-cNs frequently received contacts from tdTomato+ fibers that ascended dorsally (Figure 2J).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopic images showing contacts between labeled axons and CSF-cN cell bodies.

claim: GFP+ CSF-cN soma received multiple contacts from tdTomato+ fibers with GAD65+ presynaptic boutons.
source: We further made transverse sections from the cleared spinal cord, and confocal microscopic analyses showed that the GFP+ CSF-cN soma received multiple contacts from tdTomato+ fibers with GAD65+ presynaptic boutons (Figure 2K; Video 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data showing synaptic contacts.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV-Syn-mCherry labeled cells surrounding the ventricle in the brain, especially in circumventricular organs.
source: Indeed, we found that the intracerebroventricular injection of AAV-Syn-mCherry also labeled cells surrounding the ventricle in the brain, especially those in the circumventricular organs including the subfornical organ, vascular organ of the lamina terminalis, and area postrema, in which PKD2L1 was not expressed (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data showing ectopic labeling in the brain.

claim: A subpopulation of oligodendrocytes expresses Pkd2l1 mRNA.
source: We reassessed previously published single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing data (Russ et al., 2021), and it showed that a subpopulation of oligodendrocytes actually expressed Pkd2l1 mRNA (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of published RNA-seq data.

claim: AAV-Syn-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry injection into Pkd2l1-Cre mice specifically labeled CSF-cNs in the spinal cord without any expressions throughout the brain (cervical 100±0%, thoracic 100±0%, lumbar 99.3±0.65%).
source: We injected AAV-Syn-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry intracerebroventricularly into Pkd2l1-Cre mice, and it specifically labeled CSF-cNs in the spinal cord without any expressions throughout the brain (Figure 3H–M, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-H; PK2DL1+/mCherry+: cervical, 100 ± 0%; thoracic, 100 ± 0%; lumbar, 99.3 ± 0.65%; n=3).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative immunohistochemical data showing specificity.

claim: COX4-dAPEX2 labeled soma and ventral axon bundles of CSF-cNs.
source: Under light microscopy, it was observed that COX4-dAPEX2 labeled soma and ventral axon bundles (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents light microscopy images of DAB-stained tissue.

claim: SYP-HRP labeled dendritic bulbs, ventral axon bundles, and presumptive dorsal projections of CSF-cNs, while signals were weak in the soma.
source: SYP-HRP labeled dendritic bulbs, ventral axon bundles, and presumptive dorsal projections, while the signals were weak in the soma (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents light microscopy images of DAB-stained tissue.

claim: Some presynaptic terminals onto CSF-cNs contained COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria or SYP-HRP+ vesicles.
source: Interestingly, we found that some of them contained COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria or SYP-HRP+ vesicles (Figure 4F, G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The manuscript presents SBF-SEM data showing labeled presynaptic terminals.

claim: CSF-cNs typically received SYP-HRP+ presynaptic contacts onto the apical and basal parts of the soma.
source: It delineated apical dendritic bulbs, short dendritic structures, and basal axons, and further revealed that CSF-cNs typically received SYP-HRP+ presynaptic contacts onto the apical and basal parts of the soma (Figure 4G–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: The manuscript presents 3D reconstruction from SBF-SEM data.

claim: A prominent bundle structure composed of non-myelinated axons exists in the subependymal area and ventral funiculus, in which axons frequently contained COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria or SYP-HRP+ vesicles.
source: We found a unique prominent bundle structures composed of a number of non-myelinated axons in the subependymal area and ventral funiculus, in which the axons frequently contained COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria or SYP-HRP+ vesicles (Figure 4E, G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript presents SBF-SEM and TEM data showing unmyelinated axon bundles.

claim: Blue light stimulation evoked IPSCs in 10 of 12 Pkd2l1-GFP+ CSF-cNs with an average latency of 9.47±0.66 ms and time to peak of 5.87±1.15 ms.
source: A blue light stimulation (470 nm, 10ms) evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in 10 of 12 cells with an average latency of 9.47±0.66 ms and time to peak of 5.87±1.15 ms (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological recording data from optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The optogenetically-evoked IPSCs in CSF-cNs were blocked by bicuculline, a GABAA receptor antagonist.
source: The responses were blocked following the treatment with bicuculline, a GABAA receptor antagonist (8/8 cells; Figure 5C), indicating that the IPSCs were mediated by GABAA receptors.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing pharmacological blockade of responses.

claim: No optogenetically-evoked responses were detected in control spinal slices injected with AAV-Syn-DIO-mCherry (0/14 cells).
source: No responses were detected in the control spinal slices injected with AAV-Syn-DIO-mCherry (0/14 cells; Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents negative control electrophysiological data.

claim: Chat-GFP+ neurites and cell bodies were frequently contacted by mCherry+ CSF-cN fibers with the inhibitory postsynaptic marker gephyrin around the central canal and ventral midline.
source: We found that Chat-EGFP+ neurites and cell bodies were frequently contacted by mCherry+ CSF-cN fibers with the inhibitory postsynaptic marker gephyrin around the central canal and ventral midline (Figure 6D–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data showing anatomical contacts.

claim: Chat-EGFP+ neurites were intermingled into subependymal and ventral mCherry+ axon bundles.
source: We further observed Chat-EGFP+ neurites intermingled into subependymal and ventral mCherry+ axon bundles (Figure 6D, I–K), which may correspond to subependymal longitudinal dendrites of central canal cluster cells and medially extended neurites of medial MNs, respectively (Barber et al., 1984; Phelps et al., 1984).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data showing anatomical relationships.

claim: Some axial MN dendrites extended to mCherry+ CSF-cNs and their presumptive ascending axons at the midline and were closely contacted with presynaptic GAD65+ or postsynaptic gephyrin+ puncta.
source: Some of the axial MN dendrites extended to mCherry+ CSF-cNs and their presumptive ascending axons at the midline and were closely contacted with presynaptic GAD65+ or postsynaptic gephyrin+ puncta (Figure 6M and N, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: GFP+ MN dendrites occasionally extended and contacted in close to or within mCherry+ ventral fiber bundles of CSF-cNs, with GAD65+ or gephyrin+ puncta.
source: We further found that GFP+ dendrites occasionally extended and contacted in close to or within mCherry+ ventral fiber bundles of CSF-cNs, with GAD65+ or gephyrin+ puncta (Figure 6O, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Chx10-EGFP+ neurites ran along or across the mCherry+ fiber bundles in the ventral funiculus and were occasionally contacted with GAD65+ puncta.
source: In Chx10Cre;CAG-lcl-EGFP mice, we observed that Chx10-EGFP+ neurites also ran along or across the mCherry+ fiber bundles in the ventral funiculus and were occasionally contacted with GAD65+ puncta (Figure 6P-S).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemical data showing anatomical relationships.

claim: Some presynaptic CSF-cN terminals containing COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria contacted COX4-dAPEX2– neurites emerging from outside of the bundle.
source: We reanalyzed the SBF-SEM data of the ventral bundle, and found that some of the presynaptic CSF-cN terminals containing COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria contacted COX4-dAPEX2– neurites emerging from the outside of the bundle (Figure 6T, Figure 6—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The manuscript presents SBF-SEM data showing synaptic contacts.

claim: Rosette-like structures were found in which a COX4-dAPEX2– neurite was surrounded by multiple bouton-like presynaptic terminals containing COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria.
source: We also frequently found rosette-like structures in which a COX4-dAPEX2– neurite was surrounded by multiple bouton-like presynaptic terminals containing COX4-dAPEX2+ mitochondria along the rostrocaudal axis; this observation was also confirmed in TEM analyses (Figure 6V, Figure 6—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: The manuscript presents SBF-SEM and TEM data showing unique synaptic structures.

claim: The maximum speed to run on the treadmill was significantly decreased in CNO-treated Pkd2l1-Cre mice with hM4Di+ CSF-cNs.
source: The treadmill speed was programmed to increase from 5.0 to 35 m/min (8.33–58.33 cm/s), and it was found that the maximum speed to run was significantly decreased in CNO-treated mice (Figure 7B, Video 6).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data from DREADD inactivation experiments.

claim: Step frequencies were significantly decreased by CNO treatment in Pkd2l1-Cre mice with hM4Di+ CSF-cNs, and concomitantly, stride lengths were increased.
source: However, we found that step frequencies (Hz) were significantly decreased by CNO treatment, and concomitantly, stride lengths were increased (Figure 7D–F, Video 7).
evidence: The manuscript presents kinematic analysis data from DREADD inactivation experiments.

claim: Left-right coordination was not changed by CNO treatment in Pkd2l1-Cre mice with hM4Di+ CSF-cNs.
source: Overall, the locomotion was not abolished in the CNO-treated mice, in which left-right coordination was not changed (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript presents phase analysis data from DREADD inactivation experiments.

claim: These locomotor changes were not observed in control wild-type mice treated with AAV and CNO.
source: These changes were not observed in control wild-type (WT) mice treated with AAV and CNO (Figure 7G–K).
evidence: The manuscript presents negative control behavioral data.

claim: After CNO injections, Pkd2l1-Cre mice injected with AAV-Syn-DIO-hM4Di showed increased missed steps in the ladder walk test.
source: After CNO injections, Pkd2l1-Cre mice injected with AAV-Syn-DIO-hM4Di showed increased missed steps in the ladder walk test, while they did not show difference in the beam walk test (Figure 7L–O).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data from skilled locomotion tests.

claim: CSF-cNs are involved in sensorimotor control during skilled locomotion.
source: These results suggest that CSF-cNs are involved in sensorimotor control during skilled locomotion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ladder walk test results.

claim: CSF-cNs are facultatively involved in locomotor circuitry to control body-limb movement.
source: These results suggest that the mice with inactivated CSF-cNs are difficult to keep running on the moving belt, and that CSF-cNs are facultatively involved in locomotor circuitry to control body-limb movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the treadmill locomotion results.

claim: The intracerebroventricular AAV injection method can express any genes of interest primarily into CSF-cNs.
source: Nevertheless, the AAV-mediated method can express any genes of interest primarily into CSF-cNs; this increases specificity, depth, and diversity of the analyses.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: The combination of Pkd2l1-Cre mice and AAV-DIO improved specificity for CSF-cN targeting.
source: Thus, the combined use of Pkd2l1-Cre mice and AAV-DIO improved specificity, which would be useful for experiments requiring the strict targeting of CSF-cNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of labeling methods.

claim: CSF-cNs have ipsilateral ascending tracts in two to six segments in zebrafish larvae and frogs, suggesting conserved projection features among species.
source: It has been reported that CSF-cNs have ipsilateral ascending tracts in two to six segments in zebrafish larvae (Djenoune et al., 2017; Fidelin et al., 2015) and in frogs (Dale et al., 1987), suggesting conserved projection features among species.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and relates findings to previous literature.

claim: The rostral extensions of over 1800–4800 μm observed in mice would correspond to at least over one to four spinal segments.
source: The rostral extensions of over 1800–4800 μm observed in our study would correspond to at least over one to four spinal segments in mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured axon lengths in relation to spinal anatomy.

claim: Caudal CSF-cNs are the primary sources of GABAergic inputs to CSF-cNs.
source: These indicate that caudal CSF-cNs are the primary sources of GABAergic inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on anatomical, ultrastructural, and electrophysiological data.

claim: CSF-cNs may be involved in a motor module that controls axial muscles.
source: Our anatomical data suggest that CSF-cNs may be involved in a motor module that controls axial muscles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical connectivity data.

claim: CSF-cNs may interoceptively detect spinal bending to control axial movements.
source: CSF-cNs may interoceptively detect spinal bending to control axial movements.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: CSF-cNs may convey inhibitory signals onto a rostral motor module and also inhibit rostral CSF-cNs that sequentially release inhibitions onto a more rostral motor module.
source: CSF-cNs may subsequently convey inhibitory signals onto a rostral motor module comprising axial MN, Chat+, and V2a premotor neurons and also inhibit rostral CSF-cNs that sequentially release inhibitions onto a more rostral motor module.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: The functional effect of CSF-cN inactivation seemed to be relatively weaker compared to the phenotypes reported in zebrafish larvae.
source: Nevertheless, the functional effect seemed to be relatively weaker compared to the phenotypes reported in zebrafish larvae (Böhm et al., 2016; Fidelin et al., 2015; Hubbard et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021), as we could not see clear defects in rostrocaudal coordination or postural control.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous literature.

claim: Alternate circuits for limb control or other mechanosensory systems may predominantly work or compensate to maintain locomotion in quadrupedal species.
source: It is possible that alternate circuits for limb control or other mechanosensory systems (e.g. muscle spindles and Golgi tendons that are especially developed in mammals) predominantly work or compensate to maintain locomotion in quadrupedal species.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between mice and zebrafish.

claim: It remains unclear if CSF-cNs are fully functional or rudimentary in mice.
source: Thus, although it is phylogenetically conceivable that CSF-cNs are involved in a motor module for posture control, it remains unclear if they are fully functional or rudimentary in mice.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about CSF-cN function in mice.

claim: The study may be limited to understanding the characteristics of CSF-cN subpopulation in part, because the majority of AAV-labeled cells were located on the ventral side.
source: Our study may be limited to understand the characteristics of CSF-cN subpopulation in part, because the majority of AAV-labeled cells were located on the ventral side.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: At least two CSF-cN subpopulations, CSF-cN′ (dorsolateral) and CSF-cN′′ (ventral), have been reported in zebrafish and mice.
source: At least two CSF-cN subpopulations, referred to as CSF-cN′ (dorsolateral) and CSF-cN′′ (ventral), have been reported in zebrafish and mice (Di Bella et al., 2019; Park et al., 2004; Petracca et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In zebrafish, ventral CSF-cNs respond to longitudinal contractions, connect to CaP MNs, and are involved in fast swimming, while dorsal CSF-cNs respond to ipsilateral lateral bending, connect to putative V0-v, and are involved in slow swimming circuit.
source: Ventral CSF-cNs respond to longitudinal contractions, connect to CaP MNs, and are involved in fast swimming, while dorsal CSF-cNs respond to ipsilateral lateral bending, connect to putative V0-v, and are involved in slow swimming circuit (Böhm et al., 2016; Djenoune et al., 2017; Hubbard et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to zebrafish studies.

claim: In lampreys, lateral and ventral CSF-cNs have different mechano- and chemosensory properties, as well as the presence of motile cilia.
source: Studies in lampreys have also shown that lateral and ventral CSF-cNs have different mechano- and chemosensory properties, as well as the presence of motile cilia (Jalalvand et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a lamprey study.
